query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Intrinsic thermal expansion mismatch in the HfNbTaTiZr alloy generates persistent internal microstresses that interact with pre‐existing cold‐work induced dislocation networks and influence thermally activated recovery/segregation behavior during aging and high-temperature creep. This coupling gives rise to the observed anomalous stress–strain response (with both unexpected work hardening and softening trends) and near temperature–insensitive elastic moduli.
generation.material_initial_state: A cold-rolled, as-cast, single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy that contains dense dislocation bands from processing.
generation.intervention: Prepare two batches: a standard HfNbTaTiZr alloy and a modified version with minor compositional adjustments (or a finely dispersed secondary phase) designed to reduce the thermal expansion mismatch within the matrix.
generation.conditions: Subject both batches to in situ tensile, creep, and elastic modulus tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 1250 °C, along with controlled aging treatments at 600–800 °C. Measurements should include in situ neutron diffraction, TEM for dislocation density, and standard mechanical tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Residual dislocation networks whose density and configuration are modified by locally generated thermal microstresses arising from thermal expansion mismatch.
generation.mechanism: During cooling (or composite solidification), intrinsic thermal expansion mismatch creates localized internal stresses that stabilize or even enhance pre-existing dendritic/dislocation structures from cold rolling. At elevated temperatures, these microstresses modulate the balance between dislocation multiplication (work hardening) and dynamic recovery/recrystallization (softening) and can subtly alter elastic response, thereby unifying the disparate observations from tensile creep, aging hardening, and quasi-isotropic elastic modulus behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The batch with reduced thermal expansion mismatch will exhibit a lower residual dislocation density, a conventional temperature dependence of elastic moduli, and a more predictable work hardening-to-softening transition during creep and aging. In contrast, the standard alloy will display the anomalous, nearly temperature-insensitive elastic moduli and unconventional stress–strain behavior due to the persistent microstresses.
generation.baseline: Results reported previously for HfNbTaTiZr processed by cold rolling and aged (with observed residual dislocation bands, work-hardening signatures, and near constant elastic moduli over 293–1100 K).
generation.boundary: The unified mechanism is expected to hold for tests carried out from room temperature up to approximately 1250 °C and during aging exposures in the 600–800 °C range, provided that the alloy remains single-phase BCC without developing extensive secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thermal microstresses and their quantitative impact on dislocation dynamics remain uncertain. This hypothesis extends evidence from findings on residual dislocation effects during cold rolling (PMC10453588::web::013::3_results) and unusually stable elastic moduli (PMC11206460::web::028::characterization_of_mobile_dislocations_) by proposing that thermal expansion mismatch is the unifying factor, although this specific role was not previously tested directly. Discrepancies in the attribution of work hardening (PMC10453588::web::019::4_discussion) add further uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare and process two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one using the conventional cold rolling method (standard thermal expansion mismatch) and another with a minor compositional or microstructural modification designed to reduce the thermal expansion mismatch (for example, by adding a dispersoid or slight alloying adjustment). Subject both sample sets to identical tensile, creep, and aging tests over room temperature to 1250 °C and perform in situ neutron diffraction and TEM-based microstructural analysis.
measurements: Temperature-dependent elastic moduli from in situ neutron diffraction
Residual dislocation density and arrangement via TEM
Stress–strain curves and creep parameters (yield strength, work hardening rate, softening onset) from tensile/creep tests
Aging-induced microstructural changes (segregation, precipitation) via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy batch modified to reduce thermal expansion mismatch does not show a statistically significant change (i.e., lower residual dislocation densities, more conventional elastic modulus temperature dependence, and altered work hardening/softening behavior) compared to the standard alloy, then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch–induced microstresses govern the unified mechanical behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The differentials between the UTS and YS were about 100 MPa, and gradually widened as the temperature rose. Work hardening appeared in all curves from RT to 1073 K. We speculated that this was due to the fact that the heat treatment did not completely eliminate the residual stress of the alloy after cold rolling [,]. In order to prove this, the rolled samples were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy before a tensile test (see Figure 5). Some obvious dense dislocation bands were found in Figure 5a, and in addition, the diffraction pattern indicated that the alloy retained the structure of a single-phase BCC after the prior treatment. The region where the dislocation band was located was enlarged to further analyze its composition. In Figure 5b, it can be clearly found that the previously thought dislocation band was composed of two rows of dislocations. After a further enlargement, it was found that each dislocation band was composed of dense, short dislocations. This proved the previous conjecture that the residual dislocation after cold rolling caused a work hardening of the alloy.

Figure 9 shows the true stress–strain curves of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA at different deformation strain rates and temperatures. It was found that all curves had similar trends. That is, with the rise of the strain, the flow stress increased to the peak stress first and then decreased as the strain continued to increase. Before it reached the peak stress, the flow stress rose along with the strain. At this stage, the dislocation density increased due to deformation, the dislocation accumulation increased the deformation resistance, and a work hardening was the main rheological feature. When the flow stress achieved its maximal stress, it steadily declined as the strain increased. This is attributed to the dynamic recovery or dynamic recrystallization softening mechanism in the material exceeding the work-hardening mechanism, which is macrographically manifested as a gradual reduction in the flow stress []. In fact, the process of thermal deformation of materials is a competitive process of work-hardening and softening mechanisms, and the effects of hardening and softening reach an equilibrium when the flow stress reaches the peak stress []. cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations.
